As of 245 PM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Confidence remains very high regarding a very 
impactful storm across the region from tonight into Thanksgiving
Day with heavy rainfall and strong to damaging winds. In 
addition, there is a low-end threat for a brief tornado near the
coast from midday through the afternoon.

This afternoon, a well defined southern stream shortwave trough
over the deep south is becoming increasingly negatively tiled 
as it approaches the area from the SW. At the surface, 1040+mb 
high pressure remains anchored over New England with a ~1003mb 
surface cyclone near the east coast of Florida. Clouds continue 
to thicken over the local area well in advance of the trough, 
and light rain has started to fall in NE NC. The gradient 
between the high to our NNE and low to the south is already 
causing NE winds to gust to 20- 35 mph (highest near the coast).
Phasing of northern stream energy and the southern stream upper
trough will continue this evening- tonight, resulting in rapid 
deepening of the surface low as it lifts northward off the 
Carolina coast. The latest 12z guidance continues to show 
significant cause for concern tonight into tomorrow. A lot of 
the models show the low deepening to 993-995mb with the strong 
high remaining in place over New England. As the trough becomes 
even more negatively tilted tomorrow, the low will likely lift N
and turn NW into central NC/VA. A steady moderate rain will 
begin from S to N from now- this evening, and will become heavy 
late tonight as the low moves northward and its associated warm 
front moves toward the area. The pressure gradient will continue
to tighten by late tonight with pressure falls as high as 
16mb/6 hours on some of the guidance! These extremely impressive
pressure falls will result in strong to damaging synoptic 
winds. Northeast winds are expected to gust to 40- 50 mph inland
and 55-65 mph near the coast. While 925mb wind fields are even 
higher than this ~70 kt/80 mph, not all of this be able to mix 
to the ground. Nevertheless, expect scattered to widespread 
power outages/tree damage near the coast, with at least some 
degree of impacts inland with the higher end advisory level 
winds. Impacts in the Wind Advisory area inland will be greater 
than what occurs during our typical Wind Advisories. High Wind 
Warnings have been expanded to include all of the Northern Neck,
Middle Peninsula, and all counties bordering the James River. 
Forecast confidence in the winds is high. The strong E-NE wind 
continues for much of the morning before diminishing and 
becoming SE during the afternoon. 

The potential for widespread heavy rainfall continues, and there are 
concerns for not only convectively driven heavy rain near the coast, 
but also a band of heavy rain owing to 850mb frontogenesis across 
the Piedmont (NW of the low track). The heaviest of the rain is 
expected from late tonight-mid afternoon on Thursday. Rainfall rates 
could reach 1-2" per hour at times with embedded convection near the 
coast. Areal average rainfall of 2-5" is expected, with localized 
amounts of 6" possible. Given the above concerns, the Flood Watch 
has been expanded to include the entire CWA. Despite the very dry 
antecedent conditions, 4-5"+ of rain will be enough to result in 
flooding. Flash flooding is most likely in urban and poor drainage 
areas, especially with any remaining leaves coming down in the 
coincident strong winds and clogging drainage systems. The low moves 
into/across the region Thursday afternoon with decreasing winds and 
precip. While the very strong synoptic wind and heavy rain are the 
most widespread concerns, we are still monitoring the threat for 
severe weather. With a farther west low track, a larger portion of 
the area will get into the warm sector of the system. After the main 
area of rain exits from south to north, there remains uncertainity 
whether additional convection can develop in the warm sector during 
the midday/afternoon. Some of the models show this, while others do 
not. With temps rising into the lower 70s and dew pts in the mid-
upper 60s in the warm sector, instability is expected to increase to 
a few hundred J/kg of MLCAPE at least in SE VA/NE NC. With the 
strong kinematic fields in place and low-level winds becoming SE, 
any storm that manages to develop in the warm sector will pose at 
least a low-end threat for a brief tornado. SPC has added a Marginal 
(Level 1/5) Risk for severe weather in areas near the bay/coast in 
addition to NE NC. 
 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Significant coastal flooding is expected late tonight into 
Friday, with widespread major flooding with the Thursday morning/afternoon
cycle, potentially reaching to near-record water levels at a few locations.
